text: A physical server has one fixed set of CPU cores, one pool of RAM, and one set of physical disks. A hypervisor is the software layer that carves those fixed physical resources into multiple sets of virtual resources, handed out to separate virtual machines, each one believing it has its own dedicated hardware. Behind the scenes, the hypervisor is constantly scheduling and enforcing isolation so several VMs can safely share that one physical box.

A Type 1, or bare-metal, hypervisor installs directly on the physical hardware, with no general-purpose host operating system underneath it — the hypervisor itself is the first thing that boots. VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, and KVM built into the Linux kernel are all real examples. Because there's no host OS competing for CPU and memory, Type 1 runs at near-native performance, which is exactly what production datacenters and every public cloud provider run on their physical servers.

A Type 2, or hosted, hypervisor is just an application installed on top of a regular operating system, the same way you'd install any other program. Oracle VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are real examples — you open one on your Windows laptop, create a VM, and run a guest OS like Ubuntu inside a window. The host OS is still running underneath, competing for the same CPU and memory the VMs need, which is why Type 2 is used for development and testing on a personal machine, not production servers.

Either way, a hypervisor is abstracting the same four things: a virtual CPU scheduled onto physical cores, virtual memory mapped to physical RAM, a virtual disk backed by a file on the host, and a virtual network adapter. Every VM you'll ever touch is built from these four abstracted pieces.

That's the core distinction this whole chapter builds on. Next up, Lesson 20 goes one level deeper into exactly how a hypervisor shares CPU, memory, and storage between multiple VMs running on the very same physical hardware.
